item.title: Who gets to name the future?
item.description: Cracked, maxxed, and forward deployed: a field guide to AI’s boys’ club.My 4-year-old’s Halloween cat and the general vibe of this articleIn a single meeting recently, I heard that someone had one-shotted a prototype, that we should spin up a tiger team, and that what the customer really needed was a forward-deployed engineer.Nobody blinked. I nodded the way I nod at the dentist when he asks me a question with both hands in my mouth: agreeably, whatever, just get over with it asap, and with no idea what I had just agreed to.It only hit me later, standing in my kitchen taking a bio break, staring into the fridge as if it owed me an explanation. I had just sat through thirty minutes of something that sounded a lot like a military briefing. About…software. Delivered by people whose most dangerous mission to date was a team offsite with a dinner spend limit that was going to make including alcohol difficult.So I did what I always do when wording kinda tickles me. I went down the rabbit hole.And ladies and gents, I found some good stuff.Here’s what I found.The AI era has a vocabulary. That vocabulary has a gender. And not just that. It also has a class and a color too.It was coined by the same kind of people who coined the language of every tech wave before this one, and it’s doing what that language has always done: telling everyone else, very politely, that this room isn’t really for them.Before you come for me in the comments: I’m not innocent here. I once titled an essay Designers, we should be killing it right now. I’ve told design leaders to pick one real fight a quarter and to spend credibility like money. I talk like this too. We all do. And there’s no vaccine for this one.That’s exactly the problem.Welcome to the war room.The language of the AI era is borrowed from war rooms, Cold War think tanks, and Fortnite lobbies. Coincidence? I think not. Let’s take a look together.Forward-deployed engineer. The hottest job title in AI right now: postings grew over 1,000% year over year heading into 2026. Palantir coined it in the mid-2000s for engineers embedded with US government and defense customers, borrowing the military idea of a soldier posted in the field, close to the action. Palantir’s first FDEs were called Deltas. As in Delta Force. Now OpenAI and Google are racing to hire them. Yesterday I saw an ad for a forward-deployed creative (turns out that’s just a sales guy).Tiger team. The earliest documented use is a 1964 aerospace paper describing a team of “undomesticated and uninhibited technical specialists.” Undomesticated. Eh. The Apollo 13 rescue crew made the term famous. Today it’s what your VP says when a launch is on fire. Tigers, for the record, are solitary animals that spend a good part of the day asleep. I’m not saying that describes your tiger team. I’m saying the metaphor holds up better than anyone intended.Red team. RAND, early 1960s. The red team played the Soviets, the blue team played the Americans. Every major AI lab now red-teams its models. Useful practice. Cold War name.Blitzscaling. Reid Hoffman’s word for growth at any cost, built on blitzkrieg, the Wehrmacht’s lightning war. He has acknowledged the ugly echo and kept the name anyway. As someone who sometimes semi-identifies as German, I’d like to formally request that Silicon Valley return our words in the condition it found them. Keep kindergarten. Keep zeitgeist. Blitz comes home. Please and thank you.Frontier. As in frontier model, frontier lab etc pp. This one goes deepest. In 1945, Vannevar Bush, who helped lead the Manhattan Project, sold postwar America on science as the endless frontier, a metaphor deliberately borrowed from the closing of the American West. The frontier is America’s oldest story about men going somewhere new and claiming it. The people who were already there rarely make it into the story.I’m not loving what I’m finding so far, y’all.Forget the locker room. Welcome to the Fortnite lobby.The more ridiculous the terminology gets, the funnier its origins.One-shotted. As a verb, it comes from video games, where it means killing something with a single hit. In AI-speak, it means a model nailed the task on the first try. (The adjective is older. Its first recorded use, in 1907, was golf. Hold that thought.) Tbh I’m almost glad it’s actually a golf reference and not some new porn kink I don’t understand. But still, I wouldn’t count golf as a class-diverse sport, so there’s that.Cracked. As in we only hire cracked engineers. It’s Fortnite slang from 2019 for a player who is absurdly good, and it’s now the 10x engineer’s successor. At least one founder scrapped intern hiring entirely because no applicant was cracked enough.When I was growing up, cracked was something that happened to a phone screen, or to a person after a long winter. Or, you know, someone being hit on by David Bowie:Crack baby crack, show me you’re real.Tokenmaxxing. Most of you will know this one by now. Burning as many AI tokens as possible to climb the internal leaderboard. Meta tracked it across more than 85,000 employees. The -maxxing suffix comes straight from the manosphere, where looksmaxxing was born. It’s leaving the tap running to prove how thirsty you are. Where’s the poetry in that?996. Nine to nine, six days a week. A schedule China’s top court declared illegal in 2021, now openly advertised in AI job listings in San Francisco. Amelia Miller, who runs a platform for women returning to work, put it better than I can: 996 implies success only fits “a young, white male with an Ivy League education.” I hate this one the most for obvious reasons (hard-working mother of two).The godfathers. Hinton, Bengio, and LeCun have been called the godfathers of AI since their 2019 Turing Award. When Fei-Fei Li got the matching title, she admitted she cringed, then kept it so other women would have a voice. In 2023, the New York Times published a who’s who of AI with twelve people in it. All men. I’m in the middle of a Sopranos rewatch and now have vivid metaphors of the top AI boardrooms. Every lab has its Tony. I’d like to know who gets to be Dr. Melfi, personally.And then the two you’ve probably said yourself this week, which are sneakier:AI native. A remix of digital native, coined in 2001 by Marc Prensky, who split the world into natives and immigrants. The claims were never backed by evidence, and Prensky himself later dropped the metaphor. It’s back anyway, with a new prefix.Natives belong. Immigrants have an accent.Notice who gets to decide which one you are. It’s rarely the woman who learned the tools on parental leave with a baby on her hip. By Prensky’s logic, my daughters are AI natives. They are also native speakers of whining, which has not once helped them find their shoes in one shot.Creative technologist. The newest it title for designers and creatives who code. It grew up in advertising agencies, where one industry veteran summed up the people holding it: “in 99% of cases they were blokes.” Now the role is moving from the margins to the center of product teams, with the salary that comes with it. I have met many creative technologists. Every one of them owned a soldering iron and a strong opinion about hats. I’d love to see who gets the new offers.That being said, I also spend too much money on hats, so maybe I should accept this one.Here’s where I have to be honest.My first version of this argument went like this: these words come from the military and the golf course, and the military and the golf course are white men. Case closed.Then I checked. And, welp. It’s more interesting than that. I’d like to apologize to the golfers. (I’d like to, but I’ve seen the trousers.)Today’s US military is not the boys’ club I had in my head. Women are 17.7% of the active-duty force, 32% of service members identify with a racial minority group, and 19.5% are Hispanic or Latino. Golf, the sport of country clubs, hit records in 2025: women are 28% of on-course golfers and people of color 26%, up from 8% in 1990.Now put that next to AI.Women are a bigger share of America’s golfers (28%) than of its new AI hires (26%).And they’re hired into AI’s most coveted technical title, Member of Technical Staff, at 18%. That’s about the rate at which they serve in the US armed forces.The golf course is diversifying faster than the AI lab. The army is about as gender-balanced as the frontier lab’s engineering floor.If we’re really deciding the future now, I’d like that number to look quite a bit different.The vocabulary isn’t borrowed from today’s soldiers or today’s golfers. It’s borrowed from a mythology: the officer in the war room, the Cold War think tank, the frontiersman, the clubhouse, the teenage gamer at 2 AM.A story about who builds the future, written when the people allowed to build it were overwhelmingly white, male, and comfortable. The words keep that story alive long after the institutions themselves started changing.That’s my actual provocation: not that every soldier or golfer is a white man. That AI picked its heroes from a picture of power that even the army has outgrown.Tell me how that makes you feel. Please.Some numbers to back the vibes.AI is the best-paid corner of the job market right now: a typical AI posting lists about $177,000 versus $80,000 for everything else. Here’s who gets in.Made with ClaudeRead that fourth row again. Women label the data. Men get the engineering titles.And it’s not just who builds AI. It’s who uses it. Across 18 studies and about 143,000 people, women were roughly 20% less likely than men to use generative AI tools, and they were more likely to see using them as cheating. Even when researchers gave everyone equal access, the gap stayed. Ladies, why is our moral compass too developed?On race, the most detailed public numbers I could find are old. In 2019, the AI Now Institute reported that just 2.5% of Google’s workforce was Black, and women were 10% of its AI research staff. That I couldn’t find anything newer and as specific tells you something too. It also sucks that basically all the data I can find is US-only. It might be better or worse elsewhere, but this highlights again that a lot of important AI work is done in the US, a diversity problem in itself.Words ARE a door policy.You might be thinking: Nicole, they’re just words. Relax.Bullshit. I don’t believe in just words.In 2011, three psychologists looked at more than 4,000 job ads and found that ads in male-dominated fields used more masculine-coded words, like competitive and dominant. When they rewrote identical jobs with more masculine language, women found them less appealing. Because they didn’t picture themselves belonging. Not one participant noticed the gendered wording. A later replication found the effect held in startups specifically.Now look back at the glossary in this article. Deployed. Tiger. Blitz. Frontier. Cracked. Maxxing. Godfathers.Every one of them tells you what kind of person belongs, and what you’re supposed to do once you’re in: dominate, conquer, out-grind.That’s the whole point of a door policy. The bouncer never has to say no out loud. Not to me anyway; I’m crazy enough to get into Berghain, in case you couldn’t tell yet.I won’t claim this vocabulary causes the gaps above. But I’d bet my pottery wheel it doesn’t help, and I love that wheel more than some relatives.Women tell researchers they worry using AI looks like cheating. Meanwhile, the culture’s own slang celebrates being cracked and maxxing your way up a leaderboard. Something’s not adding up.Remember the golf? Here’s the twist.The paper that put one-shot learning on the AI map was published in 2006. Its first author: Fei-Fei Li. The godmother.The phrase the boys now use to brag about first-try prototypes came from a woman doing slow, careful research into how machines might learn from a single example, the way people do.It goes back further. During World War II, the US Army needed a machine to calculate ballistic trajectories: the ENIAC. Six women programmed it, with no programming languages and no manual, only wiring and logic diagrams. Their job title was literally computer (side note: can’t wait for humanity to come full circle and give us that cool-ass title back). When the ENIAC was unveiled in 1946, they weren’t introduced. For decades, photos of them were assumed to show models posing next to the machine. I really have no appropriate words for this one…so I'd rather not comment.Women were in the war room. Women wrote the first code for it. But they didn’t get to tell the story. And they sure as shit didn’t get to name anything.Other universes are available.If we absolutely must borrow a world, and apparently we must, can we at least shop around? I tried on a few.The gold rush. Honestly, the most accurate. Investors already call chipmakers the picks and shovels of AI. The rest writes itself: founders are prospectors, markets are claims, evals are the assayer’s office, San Francisco is a boomtown, and every pivot is a man knee-deep in a creek, insisting the next pan is the one. Love!The catch: the forty-niners were mostly men too. The twist: women in the mining towns often earned as much as the miners, or more, by feeding, housing, and clothing them. Luzena Wilson sold a hungry miner her biscuits for five dollars, opened a hotel, and became one of the most prosperous women in the territory. Sucks for her husband though, he never found the mother lode.Feeding, housing, and clothing the people who do the digging. In AI, we call that design.Star Trek. Very promising. Instead of a forward-deployed engineer, you’d send an away team: same idea, nobody gets bombed.The Prime Directive is basically an AI safety policy with better costumes. And Star Trek already did the thing I’m asking for. The original opening promised to go where no man had gone before. In 1987, The Next Generation quietly changed it to no one. A rename. On network television. Thirty-nine years ago.The catch: Starfleet is, structurally, a navy. In space. With ranks. I’m choosing to look past it.Star Wars. Honestly, tempting. Juniors become padawans, the staff engineer becomes a Jedi master, and vibes finally get the dignified name they deserve: the Force.The catch, sadly, is right there in the title (wars). Also, every AI lab insists it isn’t building a Death Star, which is exactly what you’d say if you were.The kitchen. I had high hopes for this one. Mise en place is context engineering. Tasting the sauce is an eval. 86 it is a deprecation notice. Then I looked it up: the classic kitchen brigade was designed by Escoffier after seven years as an army chef, as a chain of command. There is no escape. Even the soup has ranks for fucks sake.The garden. My personal favorite, and not only because I’ve lost control of mine. You seed an idea, prune a model, graft one system onto another, compost the prototypes that didn’t make it, and accept that some things grow on their own schedule no matter how many standups you hold about them. Hallucinations are weeds: inevitable, and you deal with them weekly. The catch: nobody has ever raised a Series A on compost. Yet.The pottery studio. I’m biased, obviously. You wedge the clay before you start, which is data prep. You center it, which is alignment, and anyone who has sat at a wheel knows centering is the hard part. You fire it in the kiln, which is deployment: the moment you stop being in control. And in pottery, cracked means exactly what it should. Something went wrong in the kiln.What the good examples share is the thing the war room lacks:They’re about making and tending, not conquering.Nobody in a garden has ever been told to dominate the market. The tomatoes wouldn’t stand for it.So let’s rename things.Naming is design. And design is our job.Designers, UX writers, conversation designers, researchers: we’re the people companies pay to decide what things are called. We name the features, the buttons, the error states, the career ladders. Many of us are women. We don’t need permission to walk into the war room.We need to stop calling it one.So here’s my proposal. Next time you hear one of these words, translate it.Made with ClaudeThe one I care most about is fluent. Native is something you either are or aren’t. Fluent is something you become. If the AI era has a door, I want it to say fluent so we can all get in.The future is being named right now.The AI era is being narrated, again, by too many white men. Not because they’re villains. Because they got to the microphone first (again, duh) and reached for the vocabulary they grew up with: the war movie, the space race, the frontier, the game lobby.The good news? Language is the cheapest thing in the world to change, and one of the most powerful. Every one of us who names things for a living can start on Monday.Women were there when the first computer was programmed. A woman put one-shot learning on the map. This time, let’s be in the room when the future gets its name.Tiger team, dismissed.Nicole is a Content Designer turned Design Director based in Stockholm, Sweden. She potters, writes poetry, and raises little girls in a house by a meadow. You can follow her writing here or get it directly to your inbox via her publication, eggwoman. Nicole is on LinkedIn. Find her portfolio at nicoletells.com.Who gets to name the future? was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Nobody asked for the sparkle button
item.description: Products ship with the same AI panel; people hunt for the off switch, and spend has outrun returns. Build features with AI, not AI features.Illustration by Jon Sabutis, built in HTML and CSSOpen any product you pay for and look at the top right corner. There is a sparkle. Behind it is a panel that slides in from the right, says “Ask anything”, and offers three suggestions you did not ask for. Close it and it comes back after the next update, sometimes with a new name.I should be the last person to complain. I write code with AI every working day. When I built 131 variations of one button to study hover feedback, a model wrote most of them. My design files are generated from code that AI wrote. I am about as far from a sceptic as a designer gets, and I still spend part of every week looking for the switch that turns a sparkle off.That is the gap this piece is about. The tools got genuinely good. The products built on top of them mostly did not, because most of them are the same product.The same product, forty timesHere is the feature. A chat panel, docked right. A text box with a placeholder in the second person. Three suggested prompts written by someone who has never used the app for real work. A sparkle icon, because the sparkle is now the universal sign for “we added it”. It summarises the thing you were already reading. It drafts the thing you were about to write. It answers questions about the page you are on, with a disclaimer that it may be wrong.I have seen that panel in a notes app, a spreadsheet, a design tool, a mail client, a team chat, a video call, a browser, a photo editor, a slide deck, a calendar, a music player and a bank. Not similar panels. The same panel. If you took the logos off, nobody on the team that built one could pick theirs out.Illustration by Jon Sabutis, built in HTML and CSSThere is a simple reason it converged. The model vendors sell the same capability to everyone, through the same API, with the same demo. A company that buys the demo and ships it has not designed anything. It has forwarded it. The feature is named after the technology, “AI assistant”, “Copilot”, “Intelligence”, because there is no user goal to name it after. Nobody ever shipped a “database feature”. They shipped search.None of this is a new observation. In 2023, before most of these panels existed, Amelia Wattenberger wrote Why Chatbots Are Not the Future and showed why a blank text box is the worst way to expose a capable model: it tells you nothing about what it can do. The same year Maggie Appleton published her Language Model Sketchbook, subtitled “or why I hate chatbots”, with three working alternatives, one of them a model that lives in the right-click menu of the document you are writing. The industry read both pieces and shipped the text box anyway.Forced on, not opted inThe part people actually resent is not that the panel exists. It is that it was turned on for them, and that off is hard to find.Microsoft is the clearest case because it is the biggest. Copilot went into Notepad, the Snipping Tool, Photos and Widgets, with the button in the toolbar and no plain way to remove it. In March 2026 the company said it would cut back on “unnecessary Copilot entry points”, starting with those four apps, and the head of Windows wrote that Microsoft would be more intentional about where Copilot goes. That is a company admitting, in public, that it had added AI to a text editor without a reason.The reaction is not confined to grumpy enthusiasts. A Hacker News thread titled “I’m drowning in AI features I never asked for and I hate it” passed three hundred points, and the top complaints were from people who use AI daily by choice: they were objecting to the version they could not decline. Outside the industry it is wider still. In Pew’s June 2025 survey, half of American adults said AI’s growing role in daily life left them more concerned than excited, against one in ten who felt the other way.Meta went further than Microsoft. In spring 2025 a blue and purple ring appeared in the WhatsApp chat list, then in the search bar, and there was no way to remove it. Meta called the feature optional. You could choose not to tap it. That is the definition of optional a company reaches for when the feature cannot survive a real one.Animation by Jon Sabutis, built in HTML and CSSEvery designer knows what a feature that people keep turning off is called. It is a bug with a marketing budget.What the loop costsThe toggle that resets is a small thing, and that is why it does so much damage. A setting is a promise. The product said “this is yours to decide”, you decided, and an update decided back. The click to fix it costs nothing. What costs is what you learn from it: this product will override me.Once learned, that rule does not stay on the one feature. Every update becomes something to audit. You stop reading release notes for what is new and start reading them for what has been done to you. People delay updates, pin old versions, and search for “disable” before they search for “how to”. That is the cognitive friction: not the dismissals themselves, but the vigilance they teach. Attention that should go to the work goes to guarding the interface.Then it moves from the product to the brand. In January 2025 Apple paused its notification summaries for news apps after the feature rewrote a BBC alert into a false claim that a murder suspect had shot himself. The summary was on by default. The mistake was the model’s, but the name on the notification was Apple’s, and the BBC complained to Apple, not to the model. A feature forced on carries the brand on every error it makes.The last stage is the strangest. In August 2024 the head of Procreate recorded a video to say the app would never add generative AI, and the artists who use it cheered. A promise not to ship a roadmap item went viral. That is what the loop buys, in the end: a market in which the absence of your feature is a selling point for your competitor.Trust is cheap to lose here for a structural reason. One forced toggle does not teach “this feature is annoying”. It teaches “this company will override me”, and a rule about the company applies to everything it ships next, including the feature that would have been good.The billSo why does it keep shipping? Because of what it cost to build the thing underneath.UBS now estimates the big cloud companies will spend about $4.1 trillion on capital expenditure between 2026 and 2028, after roughly $492 billion in 2025. In 2026 Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft together are expected to spend 102 percent of their cloud revenue on capex. Every dollar that comes in from cloud goes back out as chips and buildings, and then some.Chart by Jon Sabutis, from UBS estimates, August 2026That money has to come back from somewhere, and the somewhere is us: every product team that buys tokens and every customer who pays for the seat. Which is why the panel is on by default. A feature that is off is a feature nobody is billed for.Now put that next to what the buyers are getting. MIT’s NANDA group looked at 300 public deployments and interviewed 150 leaders, and found that 95 percent of companies saw no measurable return from their generative AI pilots. The 5 percent that did had integrated the tool into one specific workflow and learned from it. Gartner’s own number is kinder and still bleak: one in five AI initiatives delivers any measurable return, and one in fifty delivers something transformational.Chart by Jon Sabutis, from the MIT NANDA report, August 2025Is this panic?Not yet, and the word is wrong anyway. Panic is fast. What I see on product teams is slower and more embarrassing: the roadmap has an item called “AI” with no user problem under it, and for the first time someone with a budget is asking what it is for.The newest version of the item is called an agentic strategy. Everyone has one. Almost nobody who has one can show you a map of how the work in their company actually gets done: who starts a task, what they open, who they wait on, where it stalls. An agent is a worker. You cannot hire a worker for a job you have not described, and the description is the part nobody wrote.Those are the two halves of the same mistake. The spend assumed demand would appear once the capability existed. The product teams assumed a feature would appear once they had the API. Both skipped the step where you find a person with a goal and ask what would help. That step is called design, and it is the step that got cut because the board wanted the sparkle on the slide by the next quarter.Jakob Nielsen called this technology the first new UI paradigm in sixty years: you state the outcome you want instead of the steps to get there. Take him at his word and the docked panel looks even stranger. A new paradigm arrived, and the industry gave it the interface of a 1990s support chat.You can tell which features skipped it. They are the ones named after the technology. They are the ones that are on by default and hard to turn off, because a feature nobody asked for has to be forced to get used. And they are the ones whose success metric is “engagement with the panel” rather than anything the person came to do.Features with AI, not AI featuresI have one rule for my own work, and it has held up: build features with AI, not AI features.The 131 buttons were a feature built with AI. A person wanted hover feedback that answered a real question. A model wrote the variations in an afternoon so I could spend my time judging them. The person who eventually uses the button sees no sparkle, no panel, no disclaimer. They see a button that behaves well. AI is in the process, not the product.The reservation card in my last piece is the same. AI writes the states, the long French name, the failed photo, the slow network, so the design is judged in the material it ships in. Nobody on the receiving end has to know a model was involved, and nobody has to opt out of anything.The sparkle panel is the opposite shape. AI is in the product, and the process that should have come first, finding the goal, never ran.The ones you do not noticeIt is fair to ask what the other kind looks like, so here are four I use, and none of them has a sparkle on it.Gmail’s Smart Compose, from 2018, is the oldest and still the cleanest. You type, grey text appears ahead of your cursor, you press Tab or you keep typing. There is nothing to open and nothing to close. It is named after what it does, it lives in the box you were already typing in, and it does nothing until you are mid-sentence. Now look at the same inbox in 2026. A “Summarise this email” button sits on top of a three-line message. Same company, same model family, two different shapes, and only one of them was designed from a goal.Photoshop’s Remove tool is a brush. You paint over the thing you want gone and it is gone. It sits beside the healing brush it replaces, in the toolbar where that job has always been. The model is in the tool and the name is not.Figma’s rename layers command takes a chore nobody wanted and turns it into one keystroke. The result is a list of sensible names in the panel you were already looking at. No chat, no suggestions, no “Ask anything”.Descript’s remove filler words is the same shape for audio. One command, the ums are gone, and you are back in the transcript.Emily Campbell’s Shape of AI catalogues the interface patterns that have emerged around models, and it is worth an afternoon. What strikes me reading it is that the patterns that work, the ones she files under inputs and governors, are mostly invoked from inside the work, and the sparkle panel is not a pattern at all. It is a place to put the patterns you have not designed yet.What they share is easy to list. Each is named after a verb. Each lives where the work already happens. Each is invoked, so there is nothing to turn off, because it does nothing until you ask. And each solves a problem a person could have described before the model existed. The model made the solution possible. It did not pick the problem.Four questions before you ship oneIf an AI feature is on your roadmap, these are the questions I would want answered before a line of it gets built. They are ordinary product questions. That is the point.Who asked? Not “would users like this”, but which person, on which task, got stuck in a way this unsticks. If the answer is “the board”, stop.What is it named after? If the name is the technology, there is no goal in it yet. Rename it after what it does for the person. If you can’t, you don’t have a feature.Would you ship it off by default? If the feature only earns its place when forced on, it has no place. The people who want it will find the switch; the ones who don’t should never have to.Would it survive at cost price? The tokens are subsidised today by that $4.1 trillion. Price the feature as if they weren’t. If it dies, it was never worth more than its marketing.Most sparkle panels fail all four. The good AI features I have seen, and there are some, pass all four and have no sparkle on them, because they were designed the way everything else was: from a person with a goal, backwards.In the roomThe questions are easy to agree with and hard to use. I lead design at a fintech and report to the CEO, and I have no budget authority either. Here is what has worked for me when the roadmap arrives with “AI” on it and no problem under it.Do not argue with the strategy. “Should we have an agentic strategy” is a yes or no question with a board behind the yes, and you lose it in the room. Change the question to “which job”. Nobody with a strategy can object to being asked where it applies.Volunteer for the map. Offer two weeks to document how three real tasks get done today: who starts them, what they open, who they wait on, where they stall. Leadership rarely refuses, because it is cheap and it looks like progress on the strategy. The map is where an agent either finds a job or does not, and you are the one holding it. You have moved the decision from a slide to evidence without saying no to anyone.Bring the four questions as a form, not an objection. A one-page brief that every AI item fills in before it gets built. Nobody can argue against filling in a form. Items that cannot fill it in die quietly, and nobody has to be the person who killed them.Rename it in the ticket. “AI assistant” becomes “Draft the reply” or “Find the duplicate”. When there is no verb to rename it after, that shows in the ticket, and the product manager notices before you have to point.Price it. Ask what the tokens cost per seat at list price and put that beside the price of the seat. You do not need budget authority to ask a question whose answer has a currency sign on it.Propose the opt-in version as the experiment. Ship it off by default and measure who turns it on and keeps it on. That is a real signal, and it is the version you wanted anyway. If leadership insists on default-on, ask for an off switch that is one tap away and survives updates. That is a fallback you can usually win, and it protects the thing the loop above destroys.And when you lose, lose well. Ship it, instrument it with a task metric rather than panel opens, and bring the number back in a quarter. Being right in a quarter beats being right in the meeting, and it is the only kind of right that changes the next roadmap.The sparkle is a confessionNobody chose the icon on purpose, either. Fast Company traced how the sparkle took over AI and found no first use, only a drift from the emoji people used when they wrote about models to the glyph on the button, because it read as magic and nobody had a better idea. A sparkle icon tells you two things. The company has a model, and it did not know what to do with it. It is a label that says “AI goes here” in a product where nobody found the place.The investment will sort itself out or it won’t. I am not an economist, and the people who are don’t agree. But the product side is not a mystery, and it is not a bubble. It is a generation of teams that were handed a capability and told to ship it, and skipped the part of the job that would have told them where.Find the person. Find the goal. Build the feature with the AI, then take the sparkle off. Nobody will miss it.Nobody asked for the sparkle button was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Where to draw the line before AI reaches professional users
item.description: Every roadmap has a chat box on it. Fewer have an answer for who it’s for.Six questions to ask for whether a conversational layer will speed experts up or quietly put a keyboard between them and the work they already know.Nearly every B2B application I’ve seen has a chat box on it. Sometimes a sidebar, sometimes a rebuild where the prompt becomes the front door.The feature is usually well designed and has an element of sparkly craft in it, because that’s how we are defining craft in AI now, right?The question underneath it — who is this for, and what were they doing thirty seconds ago, how long have they been doing it in their career — usually goes unanswered.That question matters more in professional applications than anywhere else, because these users aren’t visitors, they expert users in very specific domains; they have spent decades learning their domain and their software.I’ve spend decades, literally, watching them and have come to the conclusion that some use cases should never be replaced by AI because it will never beat them.They’re a claims adjuster on file 82 of the week, an attorney who has read 10,000 contracts and knows the difference between assignment and change of control is just a few words they wrote in a contract 7 years ago and reuse the same pattern today, a supply planner who knows every exception code by heart. They open the same six screens every morning and know exactly where everything lives.For them, conversation is a detour through a mine laden text field for a group of users that have off the charts cognitive limits because they’ve been in their domain, forever.I know, I’ve seen it — in real time.These UX decisions are downstream of one missing step: nobody drew the line first and that line is written in pencil. The reality is that where the line is for a professional application is a bit smudged, but we still have to draw it, especially in the time of AI.Here are six considerations that tell you where the line belongs.Expertise is a skill someone already paid for. A redesign asks them to pay for it twice.Does It Break Existing Skills?An expert has built a skill inside your product — keyboard paths, saved views, the workaround they invented in 2019 they have written on post it notes shaves 90 seconds off a daily task.I’ve seen that last one much more than I would like.None of this shows up in your analytics, and all of it gets written off the day you replace the surface it lives on.The write-off is bigger than it looks, because they aren’t only learning your new screen, they’re learning a new way of working. Jakob Nielsen argues AI is the “first new UI paradigm in 60 years”, after batch processing in 1945 and command-based interaction in 1964. An industry teaches a paradigm slowly, and your users pay tuition to every product that tries.You’ll hear the resistance called sunk cost fallacy, usually as grounds to override it.Wrong label.A sunk cost shouldn’t touch the next decision. The months your user spent learning your product aren’t spent — they’re invested, and they pay out every morning, and they won’t even upgrade software to change their patterns.The users are protecting an asset. The roadmap is protecting a decision.The fallacy sits on the other side of the table. A team that funded a chat surface for two quarters, watched adoption stall and shipped it anyway is running the pattern Barry Staw documented in “Knee-Deep in the Big Muddy”: people commit the most resources to a failing course precisely when they caused the earlier losses.The expertise reversal effect names the mechanism: support that helps beginners turns costly for anyone who already knows the domain. A conversational layer is scaffolding, a gift on day one and an obstruction in year four.For example, natural language might seem cool, but the recruiter or lawyer that has 400 saved searches? They’ll want the knobs and dials because they know better than AI.The bar isn’t “better.”Say the multiple out loud: three times faster, or something the old path couldn’t do at all. If you can’t name a number, ship it beside the old path so you can learn.Graphical interfaces kept the command line for 20 years, and the people who needed it never stopped using it.Conversation lowers a barrier for people who don’t know the system. Experts have the opposite problem.Is The Chat Only for Novices?Conversation solves recall.If you don’t know a system, every menu is a vocabulary test you’re failing in public, which is why most enterprise applications are information architecture mine fields. Type a sentence instead and the burden moves to the machine. That’s a real improvement, and it’s why chat lands so well in a demo — demos are always someone’s first day.Tesler’s law names what’s actually happening: complexity is conserved. Every system has an irreducible amount of it, and the only question is who absorbs it.Chat doesn’t remove the complexity of your product, it relocates it and leverages the system to help with AI.For someone who doesn’t know the system that’s a good trade — the machine takes the part they can’t carry. For the expert it runs backwards. They absorbed it years ago, in the form of the field name and the status code, and the prompt hands it back to them as a phrasing problem.Direct manipulation solved the same problem from the other side. Ben Shneiderman’s 1983 formulation, still the cleanest definition anyone has written, put objects on screen where you could see them, act on them and undo what you did. Recognition instead of recall.For the novice, the prompt is a rescue.For the expert, it’s a translation layer over a system they already speak fluently, no matter how complex.NN/g calls the novice’s version of this the articulation barrier — people know what they want, can’t phrase it, and get generic results back. Experts have the reverse problem. They know the field name, the status code, the exact filter, and are much faster with it.Asking them to describe it in a sentence doesn’t lower a barrier, it builds one in many cases. Test accordingly.Do Users Need to See the Whole Set?Here’s what filters do that a prompt can’t: When an adjuster narrows a queue to 12 open files, they don’t just get 12 files, they learn there are 12 and not 400, that three are past SLA, and that the pattern looks like a Tuesday last November.None of that was the question, all of it is the answer and scanning is diagnosis.Filtering is a hypothesis you can run in half a second and abandon just as fast, which is why experts sweep through six before committing to one. A chat response hands back a result without the shape of what surrounds it.A chat answer tells you what you asked for; a screen tells you what you should have asked.Linus Lee made the harder version of this point in 2022: conversations are a bad way to keep track of information, because the state you need ends up in scroll back instead of in front of you.Screens also carry something transcripts don’t — a shared model. Two people looking at the same view see the same thing, and they can point. A conversation is private by construction, so every user builds their own path and nobody can audit it.Fine for a consumer app but a real problem in an operations team of 40. That’s why AI search may not be the answer.Experienced developers in METR’s trial were 19% slower with AI, and believed the opposite.Does It Slow Experts Down?METR ran a randomized trial with experienced open-source developers on their own repositories and found them 19% slower when allowed to use AI tools. The part that should worry you more: they expected a 24% speedup going in and still believed they’d gotten one coming out. They could not feel it happening.Small sample, one kind of work, so don’t over-read it. It rhymes with the largest field experiment we have. Dell’Acqua, Mollick, Lakhani and their co-authors put 758 consultants through the jagged technological frontier study: inside AI’s capability, subjects were 25.1% faster at higher quality; on tasks just outside it, 19% less likely to be correct than the control.Expertise is already compression. A prompt asks the expert to decompress it into English so the machine can compress it back.Watch a partner who has drafted the same indemnity clause 200 times. They don’t compose it, they recall it, and the recall is close to instant, nuance is more real than AI understands, and they have to write it in the spirit of the original language.The prompt-read-correct loop costs them more than that and leaves them less certain than when they started, because now they’re checking someone else’s work instead of trusting their own.The model isn’t bad. They’re very good, and the interface asked them to slow to the speed of a sentence.How Hard Is It to Verify?In professional work an answer isn’t finished when it appears. It’s finished when someone has checked it and will put their name on it. That cost never shows up in the demo.Stanford researchers tested the purpose-built legal research tools — the ones sold specifically as grounded and reliable — and found Lexis+ AI and Thomson Reuters’ tools hallucinating between 17% and 33% of the time.Better than a general chatbot.Nowhere near good enough for an associate to stop reading every citation, which means the associate is still reading every citation.The more an output has to be defended to a third party, the worse a chat box performs as the place to make it.Chat is structurally poor at supporting the check. It returns prose, and prose flattens the difference between what was retrieved and what was generated. A filtered result is auditable by construction — the query sits in the chips above the table, and anyone can rerun it.Ask who has to defend the output: the further an answer travels, the more the surface has to show its work.Three destinations, and only one of them is a chat box.Where Should the Work Go?None of this means don’t build it. It means work has three destinations and only one of them is a chat box.Routine Tasks Stay in the InterfaceThe first destination is the queue somebody works 200 times a day, the saved views, the keyboard path they could walk in the dark. Repetition is what buys speed here, and the speed is the product.Cost runs the same direction and catches teams out: a click costs nothing to serve, while a prompt against the core loop bills you every time someone does what they used to do for free — which is why cost heads Gartner’s list of reasons these projects get cancelled.Put a text field in front of the daily queue and you’ve charged your best users a tax to use their own product.Rare Tasks Go to ChatThe second is the long tail nobody would design a screen for. Which of these 400 contracts have a change-of-control clause and a non-standard liability cap. One-offs that cross the whole schema and become a ticket to an analyst who answers in three days. Answers that are anomalies deep in the financial analysis.That’s where conversation is worth real money, because the alternative isn’t a filter because it’s a wait, and a question asked once a quarter is worth paying per call for.Call it the ticket test.If the user would have filed a ticket, chat is competing against three days and the bar is low. If they would have clicked, it’s competing with muscle memory, and muscle memory is undefeated.Ongoing Tasks Go to an AgentThe third destination is the one teams keep missing, and it isn’t a conversation at all.A contract arrives with a non-standard cap.A shipment slips its window.An account’s usage drops three weeks running.Nobody needs to type a question about any of these, because the system already knows. That work belongs to an ambient agent running against the same data your screens display, interrupting only when a person has to decide something.The idea isn’t new. Christopher Noessel called these systems agentive a decade ago in “Designing Agentive Technology”, and Golden Krishna argued for background processes over screens in “The Best Interface Is No Interface” in 2015. The models are finally good enough to make it work.Chat waits to be asked. An ambient agent already knows.Chat is pull and needs the user to know a question exists. Ambient is push and needs the system to be right about what deserves attention, which is the harder problem and the better product. Get it wrong and you’ve built a notification nobody trusts, so tune for precision and let the agent stay quiet. Get it right and it does the scanning nobody can do at 3 a.m., then hands back a filtered queue — which is to say it ends where the interface begins.ConclusionThe line has nothing to do with how you feel about conversation. It’s a question about who’s standing in front of the screen and how many times they’ve done this before.The truth:Novices need language —they don’t have the map nor the dictionary.Experts have the map — they built it, they maintain it, and every screen in your product is a landmark on it.Handing them a text box asks them to give up the map and describe the terrain instead, to someone who’s never been there and occasionally makes places up.So run the checklist before you run the sprint. Answer the five questions honestly, on real usage data rather than the demo in your head, and the roadmap sorts itself.What’s left is a smaller chat feature than the one you were planning, aimed at work your users currently can’t do at all, sitting beside an interface you didn’t have to apologize for and an agent quietly working the queue while nobody’s watching. That’s a better product than a prompt on top of everything. It’s also harder to demo, which is most of the reason it doesn’t get built.ChecklistThe six tests reduce to five questions. They’re abstract on purpose — they should still work after the next model release, and the one after that. Saleema Amershi, Mihaela Vorvoreanu and their colleagues at Microsoft Research validated 18 guidelines for human-AI interaction against 20 shipping products in 2019. These five are narrower, and only settle whether a conversation belongs in front of an expert at all.How well does this person already know the system? Everything else follows from this one. Language helps whoever lacks the map and gets in the way of whoever drew it.Is this task routine, rare, or continuous? Routine work belongs to the interface, where repetition buys speed. Rare work belongs to conversation, because nobody was ever going to build a screen for it. Continuous work belongs to an agent that watches and interrupts, because nobody should have to remember to ask.Does the user need an answer, or the shape of the whole set? Retrieval is a question with a reply. Diagnosis is a question about what surrounds the reply, and it needs a surface that shows the surroundings.Who is faster here, and who is more certain? Speed without certainty isn’t speed. It’s a cost that shows up later, in the time it takes someone to trust the output enough to sign their name to it.Is it worth what switching costs? Every new path bills the user for the old one they’d already mastered. If you can’t say plainly how much better this is, leave the old path where it is and let them choose.Action ItemsPut chat where the tickets are. Pull 90 days of requests your customers sent to analysts and operations; that queue is a validated feature list with volumes already attached.Give every answer a screen to land on. Render results as a filtered view the user can adjust, save and share, so the conversation hands off to the interface instead of replacing it.Measure verification time, not generation time. Track how long it takes a user to trust an answer enough to act on it, and whether that number is falling.Find the alerts nobody set up. Ask your users what they check by hand every morning, and what they wish someone had told them last week. Each answer is an ambient agent with a job and an audience already attached that wants to be helped.Watch the fallback ratio. Keep the clicking path and track which one users reach for. That ratio is what they actually think of the feature, and it won’t match what they say in a research session.Where to draw the line before AI reaches professional users was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Entering Atomic Design from the screen
item.description: You don’t always have to build from atoms. Sometimes, you need to discover them.Atomic Design is one of the core mental models of modern design systems. It gives us a common language for describing the interface as a hierarchy: atoms, molecules, organisms, templates, and pages.Brad Frost said from the very beginning that atomic design is not a linear process, but a mental model that allows us to keep both the whole and its parts in view at the same time. The five levels are not steps one through five.From Template to Atoms.However, in practice, most teams apply the model in one direction. This is especially true when they aim to build a component library: they define the smallest reusable parts and assemble larger blocks from them. And the begin to use them all in screens.This habit is so common that many people mistake it for the methodology itself.Product work usually starts from the other side — from the user experience. When we look at a screen, the first question isn’t “what components are used here,” but “what does the user need to do here?” How will they search, filter, compare, select, edit, and so on?This is another entry point into the Atomic Design model. We could say that this is a “scope-first” approach.A component-first approach can obscure the actual structureA “component-first” approach usually begins with an inventory:This is a buttonThis is an inputThis is a badgeThis is a tableThere are two well-known methods that handle this very well: Brad Frost’s Interface Inventory and Nathan Curtis’s Component Cut-Up Workshop. Both are excellent for their intended purpose: describing an existing interface and kicking off the work on the component library.Interface InventoryThe Component Cut-Up WorkshopBut they answer a specific question: “what’s on the screen?” We need to think about the rest ourselves: ”why something is there and what it’s connected to”.Let’s take a typical admin screen with a data table as an example.The user inventory here looks pretty good:Page titlePrimary actionsTab navigationSearch inputFilter inputsSort buttonsPaginationTooltipsetc.What remains behind the scenes is how all of this is interconnected:The status badge is associated with a single row.Sorting rearranges all rows in the dataset. Even though the control itself is located within a single column header.Search and filters change which records are displayed on the screen at all.A primary action like Add people affects the entire page.Tabs can completely replace the content area’s contents.The proximity of elements to one another is a poor guide in all of this. The sort button is the most obvious example: it resides in a column header but affects the entire table. Elements are linked not by their location, but by the scope of their behavior.Thinking in scopesWhen breaking down a screen, we can start with the scope of each action — the set of data or part of the interface that changes when the user triggers that action.For the admin screen above:This isn’t a complete breakdown, but it already highlights a couple of important points.First: each row in the left column answers the same question — what is changing?You might be tempted to add categories like “navigation” or “table header,” but these describe what the control is or where it’s located. That’s a different axis, and mixing the two axes is exactly what will cause the exercise to quietly turn back into an inventory breakdown.Second: tooltips and badges have no scope at all. They don’t change anything. They’re included in the table to indicate that something isn’t a control — just to complete the picture.This breakdown isn’t universal. On a different screen or in a different product, the scopes will be different.It’s not the list that’s carried over, but the process:Start with what the user can do and what they can interact with.Determine what each specific user action will affect.Decide which level should own the logic.This way, we get a structural model of the screen even before we start creating components.Where the logic livesWhen we design components, we think about the library: its versatility, independence, and applicability in contexts we cannot predict.When we design a product, we think about business logic — the parts must come together to form a cohesive user experience.Search, filters, and pagination illustrate this tension quite clearly. As library components, they can appear in different combinations on different screens, so it makes sense to keep them independent.But on this admin screen, they manage a shared dataset:Changing a filter can reset pagination to the first page.A search query with no matches empties the table, and pagination becomes unnecessary.It is impossible to list all such scenarios when documenting individual components, and the components themselves should not be aware of them. The moment the filter component becomes aware of the pagination component, it loses its reusability and begins to carry the business logic of a single specific use case.But something has to manage these connections. In my experience, it’s most convenient to do this at the template level.A slightly different view on the role of a templateIn Atomic Design, templates are page-level objects that position components within a layout and define the content structure: they are about structure, not state.To put it very simply, a template acts as a “dumb” (presentational) component that only knows how it looks and what data it receives from outside.“Smart components” (container components) are capable of managing data, state, and behavior. They are often built as wrappers around “dumb” (presentational) components.This is roughly what I suggest doing with templates. The individual components remain “presentational”: a table knows how to render rows, a filter knows how to return a value, pagination knows how to display a page number — and they’re all independent and unaware of each other. The template is the wrapper that unites them and holds the logic for how they work together.For data-dense product screens, the template level is the natural place not only for layout, but also for:Which zones are on the screen and where they are located.How the zones are connected.The shared state that flows between them.Rules that belong to the screen’s context, rather than to any specific component.I have often seen developers on product teams create wrappers around several library components when they need to reuse the same set of features, such as filters, search, tables, and pagination, that behave as a single unit.Of course, this kind of logic can be documented as a story in Storybook, but developers often prefer to keep it as ready-made modules rather than rebuilding it from scratch every time.Sometimes these wrappers appear spontaneously and end up somewhere in the /components directory alongside buttons and other “presentational” components. However, it’s still better to keep such templates separate.I should clarify: I’m not saying that every template must contain logic or that any logic should be dragged into a template. The criteria are the same as the question about scope:If a rule describes a relationship between areas and is repeated from screen to screen (“changing the filter resets pagination to the first page”), it belongs in a template.If a rule applies to a specific screen and specific data (“disabled users cannot change their role”), that’s at the page level, and the template shouldn’t be touched.A template that knows too much stops being reusable.I believe this is more of an extension than a contradiction to the logic of Atomic Design templates. This is also the clearest distinction between this approach and Component Cut-Up:Cut-up helps the team identify recurring visual elements and turn them into a list of potential components.A scope-first analysis helps understand “what a user can do on the screen, what their actions affect, and which level should be responsible for it”.Same template, different realityA good template is a reusable structure that works across different product contexts. For example, the same template can be used to manage Members, Projects, Invoices, and other pages.The zones remain the same:Page headerPrimary action areaNavigationToolbarContent areaWhat changes are the elements within them: same structure, different content and behavior.This is the moment when a design system becomes more than just a set of components and begins to describe product patterns. This is exactly what most product teams need.Checking the breakdown with real contentAt the page level, we populate the templates with actual content. At this stage, we need to stress test the system and our layout to make sure the structure can handle content it might not have been designed for. Not just for the “happy path,” but also when:When there is no data. For example, when a search query returns no results.While data is loading.When the page opens on a small screen.The text is much longer than intended for the layout.These are just a few scenarios for a particular single screen. Some of them are typical, such as the empty state. Others may be specific. It’s similar to what QA does with edge cases: finding where things break.The difference lies in what “breaking” means. It’s not always a design problem. Often, it’s a sign that the breakdown is incomplete: a certain state or part of it has no owner, or a rule hasn’t been defined for the zone in case it’s empty.When this approach is useful?First, when you need to create a design system for an existing product. When the product already exists, the question isn’t “How do we create components from scratch?” but rather “How do we understand and systematize what already exists?”Second, when there are debates about the boundaries of components. A scope-first breakdown provides both sides with a more neutral way to discuss ownership. Instead of arguing about whether something “looks like” a component, the team can discuss what it affects and which level should own that behavior.Third, when a product has many similar screens. Admin panels, dashboards, CRM tools, settings pages, marketplaces, financial tools, and internal platforms often repeat the same patterns with different data. Scope-first approach helps clarify which parts are truly reusable and which are simply visually similar.And finally — documentation. Product patterns are much easier to describe in terms of their scopes — page actions, object actions, states. Not through a flat list of components. And this is closer to how a user perceives the screen.When this approach doesn’t help?This approach isn’t one-size-fits-all, and based on my experience, I can point out at least two ways to mess it up.The first is to adjust the logic and components to fit a single screen. The temptation is understandable: if the scope model just fits perfectly, you may want to build a library around it. But a screen is a specific use case, while components should live longer. A scope indicates the level at which the logic should reside. It says nothing about how versatile the component itself will be. I’ve encountered this situation very often when product teams were working under pressure, and designers and developers tried to save every new pattern as a component or a design system template.The second is breaking down what’s already clear. On a landing page, settings form, or login screen, the scope map takes up a single line, yet it can still take a long time to analyze. The entire approach rests on two things: screen density and the overall flow between zones. If neither is present, a traditional inventory cut-up will be faster and deliver the exact same result.ConclusionAtomic Design is a versatile model that makes it quite easy to build component libraries. However, teams often try to use it to build interfaces from small parts, taking the “atomicity” of the approach too literally.Day-to-day product work often starts from the other end: a complex screen already exists, and it needs to be understood. This article shows that Atomic Design helps with this as well. Moreover, the result is not just a more precise breakdown into components, but also a clearer understanding of the product pattern behind the screen.For product teams, this is usually what matters most.Thanks for reading! Write in the comments what you think about the topic.Let’s stay in touch! Connect with me on LinkedIn and follow me here on Medium for more design-related content.Entering Atomic Design from the screen was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

item.title: Supersonic dreams: how post-war France invented the future, and then stopped
item.description: Concorde, nuclear power and Minitel took three different paths. What can they tell us about Europe’s next technological bets?Concorde, nuclear power and Minitel. AI-generated IllustrationI’ve spent the last week walking the streets of Marseille, indulging in my long-desired vacation. My routine was simple and mostly included booking tables at local spots, open for unapologetically short hours. A sense of urgency is a funny concept when applied anywhere in southern Europe. Born & raised in a southern European city, I can really say that.At the Airbnb where I am staying, the skyline is surprisingly busy. The dense, almost panoptical view makes me think about an interesting thing. I wonder whether the atmosphere that I would describe as “clinically relaxed” was different in the past.France in the 1970s was just peak. Unlike today, it was leaping ahead on a bunch of different tracks where bold vision, execution speed and big capital mattered. It was a tight race, and the French were taking the corners perfectly, often taking the lead over the Soviets and Americans.https://medium.com/media/314577821abd2d41fb53a0dda13aa52f/hrefThe thirty years after WW2 are widely known as Trente Glorieuses or “Three Glorious Decades”. Of course, this era was not as perfect as French history documentaries may portray it. France went through a fair share of political crises when re-establishing itself politically, as well as a couple of ugly (post-)colonial wars. Yet eventually, long-lasting peace and transatlantic partnerships finally gave the continent the time and security needed for generational moonshots.Unlike Germany, which was torn in two and heavily destroyed, France enjoyed a more pleasant type of integration and the luxury of deciding its own destiny. That included nationalising critical industries, obtaining nuclear arms and racing towards the edge of technological success.By the late 1970s and early 1980s, French advancements were just bold. One of the quickest nuclear build-ups in history laid the foundations of French energy independence that endure to this day. Minitel — a French version of the internet, before the World Wide Web took over. And of course, a symbol of the supersonic dream: Concorde. Three bold bets on the future. One became a luxury, one became infrastructure, and one became obsolete.Concorde: ahead of timeIf there were ever a thing that I’d be willing to blow an unreasonable amount of money on immediately — it would be a Concorde flight. As a kid with parents in aviation, I am not easily surprised by anything flying, yet Concorde is something different.Six Concordes parked on the apron. Photo courtesy of British Airways; supplied for editorial use.Technically, it wasn’t all French: the two manufacturing facilities were located in Britain and France. That required a lot of coordination and joint effort, yet the French were never shy about taking credit for it.The plane itself was incredibly sophisticated. There was a mechanism for changing the position of the nose section on every take-off and landing to give the pilots a clear view of the runway. Flying at supersonic speeds made the outer surface so hot that the whole plane would actually extend by tens of centimetres during the flight. Also, fuel would be pumped from one tank to another mid-flight to balance Concorde’s centre of gravity.Concorde’s first test flight, Toulouse-Blagnac, 2 March 1969. Photo: André Cros / Archives municipales de Toulouse, 53Fi1931, CC BY-SA 4.0.Concorde could let you beat the clock. With a flight time of around three and a half hours and New York five hours behind London, you could leave at noon and arrive at 10:30 am local time. The whole idea of stitching together the two sides of the Atlantic with a fast-track channel in the air was futurism in reality, a testament to post-war prosperity and a true European “Ad Astra” moment.The cabin was narrow, with just four seats across. Yet it was still a more prestigious flight, with Champagne, caviar and a certificate for breaking the sound barrier. Passengers would sit next to the tiny windows and enjoy watching the plane reach a supersonic speed of Mach 2 live on the built-in indicators. In the 1990s, designer Andrée Putman redesigned Air France’s cabin, using light and restrained details to make the small space feel elegant.Champagne service aboard a British Airways Concorde. Source: Heritage Concorde.Celebrities loved Concorde. No private jet could match the vibe of a cutting-edge aviation unit, leaping forth ahead of its time. Among its passengers were Mick Jagger, Paul McCartney, Catherine Deneuve and, of course, members of the British royal family.Fred Finn beside a Rolls-Royce, with a British Airways Concorde behind him. Source: Gentleman’s Journal.The final flight of Concorde took place on November 26, 2003, when it flew to Filton for preservation. Commercial services had ended the previous month. Its demise had no single cause. Instead, it was a mix of circumstances, including the famous jet crash of 2000, a shrinking market and rising maintenance costs. The oil crisis of 1973 had already made the economics of supersonic travel harder, long before the final retirement. Add to this a limited number of routes (sonic booms restricted supersonic flying over land) and you get the reason why Concorde became a piece of the future that was no longer economically viable.Nuclear: an atomic ramp-upBack in Marseille, I’m pulling out my phone, which I’ve set to a radical “do not disturb” mode, to check the map, as we’re heading to the beach. One of the push notifications that somehow invades my attention span is about upcoming spikes in energy costs. I put my sunglasses away to figure out the route and instinctively dive into noisy news blurbs, wondering if my electricity bill is gonna hurt after I’m back home in Berlin.My electricity bill might be lower if I decided to settle in France. Energy price shocks are hardly new to the French. Back in the seventies, France already had a nuclear industry when oil prices skyrocketed. The crisis then pushed the country to accelerate its reactor build-out.The idea of strategic autonomy and the notion of self-sustaining politics were cornerstones of post-war France. This was the reason why such assertiveness in both the military and civilian parts of the economy was taken to a higher level. Ironically enough, the heart of the nuclear programme ran on American hardware. France had already built reactors of its own design, but chose a different technology for the expansion. In 1969, the final decision to use PWRs under a Westinghouse licence was reached. Later on, the reactors were adapted and “franced” — by the 1980s, production had achieved a reasonable degree of local autonomy.Flamanville nuclear power station under construction, August 1980. Photo: Jacques Lemière / Archives départementales de la Manche, fonds 115 Fi. Source.The build-out itself was carried out in the same manner as all the other post-war transformations: centralised, strategic, massive. EDF (Électricité de France) was basically the state-owned national utility. To fund its enormous effort, it was authorised to borrow enormous sums. The amount of borrowed capital was so huge that by 1976, EDF was the third-biggest borrower on the US capital market — right after Ford and General Motors.Make no mistake — France did not predict the oil crisis, nor did it slide through it. At the time, the energy price spikes did really bite. Yet in March of 1974, when then-prime minister Pierre Messmer announced an acceleration of the build-out, there was infrastructure in place to be accelerated.The build-up wasn’t flawless: the speed and the directive manner backfired, sparking various protests across the country. One major flashpoint was Superphénix — a new form of reactor that ran on the principle of “fast” neutrons and used a much newer and more experimental technology. Yet it wasn’t the only thing people were mad about.It was the non-consensual policy that made people angry: both intellectuals and the working class from rural areas. Specifically, this happened at Plogoff, near Pointe du Raz, where EDF was planning a four-reactor nuclear power station. The locals viewed this as a risk of land expropriation and disruption to fishing. Soon enough, the protests spun out of control, and after years of tension, the project was called off in 1981.Anti-nuclear campaign posters from Plogoff: boycott, confrontation and solidarity. Source: SKREO-Dz. The first two also appear in Plogoff’s municipal archive; the third is credited to Pierrick Le Corre by Musée départemental breton.Nuclear power was probably France’s most successful 1970s bet. Energy security drove the programme; lower-carbon electricity became another lasting benefit. Yet it became a backbone of the country’s autonomy and reduced volatility & external dependence, setting France apart from its neighbours.French electricity production, 1980–2023. Chart: Theanphibian / Wikimedia Commons, public domain. Data: U.S. Energy Information Administration.To this day, French power plants are monuments to Cold War-era futurism that actually became part of the economy and didn’t disappear. And surprisingly, some of them look really nice for the industrial monstrosities those things are always considered to be. It could be the beautiful landscape around them that is doing the job, or the more elegant architecture the French are famous for. But probably both.Paluel nuclear power station, Normandy, 2005. Photo: Francis Chanteloup (EDF) / Energi-vore, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0.Cruas-Meysse nuclear power station, 2012. Photo: Yelkrokoyade / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0.Minitel: online before the webI’m trying to get a table at Le Ventre de l’Architecte at the famous Le Corbusier house. The opening hours are wild: 12–2 pm, 7:30–9:15 pm, meaning you’d better get hungry when the place is open. After reading a bunch of unhinged comments from the restaurant manager (check their reviews on Google, it’s just fire), I navigate to the website. As a person who led a premium web studio, I am disappointed but not surprised by what I see. A question that pops up in my mind: was the French internet any good?Spoiler: hell yes.When we think about the early days of the internet and picture its mass adoption, we immediately imagine the US. Yet France brought online services into millions of homes well before the web became an everyday habit.Minitel was a European predecessor of the World Wide Web. It kicked off at the beginning of the 1980s. As a telephone subscriber, you could get one of the Minitel terminals for free. This wouldn’t be a regular PC: no apps or games on the device, just a b&w text interface for online services. Its design had practical limits: screen designer Jean-Yves Michalik described the 40-column display and an alphabetic keyboard that was later replaced with AZERTY.Thomson terminal used in the Télétel trial, Vélizy, 22 November 1980. Photo: Bernard Marti, CC BY 3.0.Minitel terminals were originally a fancy replacement for the paper directory. People would get hooked on additional functions like purchasing train tickets or making bookings pretty randomly, after their usual phone number searches. Apparently, this was a great strategy for adoption: by 1989, France had around five million Minitel terminals. By 1993, that figure had grown to almost 6.5 million, with terminals in 20% of households.https://medium.com/media/32699826694b1587b4b4312597f62cc3/hrefMinitel was no random accident. It was part of a visionary digital transformation, imagined, described and delivered by the French state in order to bring a futuristic reality into everyday life. “The Computerisation of Society”, a report that came out in 1978, explored the emergence of an information society. The report contained a blueprint of how the mass adoption of computers would shift many gears in societal interaction, how business would change and how politics would follow. It also considered the infrastructure and political choices that this transformation would require.That report captured the ambition behind France’s push into networked computing.One of the things Minitel would give birth to was anonymous dating chats. Or, as they called them, “pink chats”. Users would assume they were speaking with someone who was who they said they were, which was not always the case.Minitel’s early success did not turn into global dominance. Its dedicated terminals and centrally organised network made online services accessible, but eventually faced competition from personal computers and the open web. An OECD assessment pointed to ageing technology, high usage charges and limited export markets. The system that had made getting online simple also had limits.The last official year of Minitel was 2012. That was a surprisingly long life for a network born at the beginning of the 1980s.Nowadays: winds of European tech sovereigntyOne thing that caught my eye in Marseille was how many things are called “Mistral”, from navy ships you can see docked in the harbour to local soda brands and driving schools that have this word in their name.It’s a special, even holy word for many francophones. Mistral is the name of a strong, cold & mighty Mediterranean wind that blows all across Provence.Also, Mistral is the name of one of the few European frontier AI labs. As I write this text, the fourth generation of its Large model has been announced, adding another chapter to France’s ambitions in computing.Mistral AI Now Summit, Paris, 28 May 2026. Source: Mistral AIIt’s too early to predict whether the new European bet on open-weight sovereign models and an application layer for robotics and manufacturing will win the future.But at least we know that writing the future was once in fashion in Europe.Why not again?Further readingBritish Airways: Celebrating Concorde — the aircraft and its service history.Andrée Putman: Le Concorde Air France — the cabin redesign.IAEA: France country profile — the nuclear programme and reactor choices.Archives départementales du Finistère: Plogoff — the proposed plant and opposition.OECD: Minitel assessment — adoption, economics and limitations.Jean-Yves Michalik: Minitel screen design — a contemporary practitioner’s account.Supersonic dreams: how post-war France invented the future, and then stopped was originally published in UX Collective on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.
